strengths: The task addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and visual-only instance tracking: distinguishing individual sounding objects while maintaining their identities over time. AVISeg contributes 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, 94,074 masks, and 26 categories across four scenarios. This substantial benchmark contribution, together with the supported baseline improvements, favors weak acceptance.

The improvements are corroborated by established metrics. Under the stated common ResNet-50 backbone and 48,000-iteration training protocol, AVISM achieves 40.57 mAP versus COMBO's 37.84, and 61.73 HOTA versus VITA's 57.48 (Table 2). Improvements in both detection and association accuracy strengthen the evidence beyond the proposed FSLA metric.

The component ablations support the usefulness of temporal audio-visual fusion. Adding the video-level fusion module to the frame-level fusion model increases mAP from 39.06 to 40.57 and HOTA from 59.59 to 61.73 (Table 4). Window-size and pretraining experiments further characterize the baseline's behavior.

The pipeline diagrams make the approach reasonably clear. The supplement supplies several implementation details, external-model prompts, qualitative comparisons, and explicit failure cases involving multiple same-category sound sources, which help readers understand practical limitations.
weaknesses: FSLA has a substantive specification and reproducibility problem. Section 3.2 requires correct object counts, categories, and localization, but Algorithm 1 counts silent frames as correct unconditionally, omits explicit count/category checks, and initializes counters outside the threshold loop. Its frame-based aggregation also does not implement the described class averaging. Taken literally, this algorithm cannot explain the varying FSLAn results in Table 2. The reported FSLA scores therefore cannot be reliably reproduced from the supplied specification, although the mAP/HOTA results independently support the baseline.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently substantiated for a central dataset contribution. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted annotation and repeated manual review, but provides no agreement measurements or quantitative quality audit. The decision procedure for attributing ambiguous sounds to individual same-category objects, and for labeling activity transitions within one-second snippets, remains unclear. These omissions limit confidence in the claimed annotation quality.

The large-model conclusions exceed what the adaptations establish. Section 11 restricts Sam4AVS to the top-one audio category, merges same-category masks for Sam4AVS and BuboGPT, and treats each category as one instance for AL-Ref-SAM 2. These choices structurally restrict same-category instance recovery. Table 3 demonstrates limitations of these particular pipelines, but does not isolate general limitations of the underlying multimodal models.

Evidence for the strongest temporal-grounding claims is incomplete. Evaluation uses 1 FPS sampling, and Table 5 mainly establishes maximum frame capacity and window-size effects. There is no matched short-context comparison, accuracy breakdown by video length, or quantitative analysis of same-category activity switching. The audio ablation demonstrates aggregate utility, but without an audio-misalignment control it does not establish how strongly predictions depend on correctly synchronized audio.

Algorithmic originality is modest: object-token compression, shifted-window association, and query-based mask prediction substantially follow VITA and Mask2Former, with audio cross-attention added. This is reasonable for a benchmark baseline, but places the main scientific contribution in the task and dataset. A smaller technical correction is also needed in Section 3.2: mAP can penalize non-sounding false positives, so the blanket claim that such predictions do not decrease mAP is incorrect.
